the_standard: Every app's staging runs in one GCP project. Production stays in the project that already runs that app.
why: Developers can verify a change without holding production credentials, and a staging mistake does not land in the warehouse, commerce, or finance production projects.
how: Create the project, attach billing, and use its id as the staging_project input on the plan and deploy workflows. New apps do not get a personal project.
tech_stack: GCP. The draft name is opptra-staging.
example: gcc-dashboard staging is a Cloud Run service in opptra-staging. Production stays in the project named in that repo's service.yaml.

step: Bootstrap identity, state, and the image registry
the_standard: GitHub authenticates with Workload Identity. Terraform state lives in a versioned bucket per project. Images live in one Artifact Registry repo named apps, in asia-south1. Budgets notify at 50, 90, and 100 percent.
why: The plan can only add, change, and destroy what is recorded in state. A key file in GitHub is a credential that can be copied. The budget is how a shared staging project gets noticed before it runs away.
how: A person follows docs/gcp-bootstrap.md once: enable APIs, create the pool opptra-github, create gs://<project>-tfstate with versioning, and create the apps repository. The same bucket pattern is repeated in each production project.
tech_stack: Workload Identity Federation. Cloud Storage. Artifact Registry. Cloud Billing budgets.
example: State for gcc-dashboard in staging is the object prefix gcc-dashboard inside gs://opptra-staging-tfstate.

the_standard: Each repository impersonates its own deployer service account in staging and in its production project. Humans do not have deploy roles.
why: The workflow then has a named identity, and a person with a laptop cannot ship production beside it.
how: Run scripts/bind-repo.sh with the GitHub repo and the prod project id. Set the four Actions variables it prints. The script creates the deployer only. The first Terraform apply creates the Cloud Run service.
tech_stack: scripts/bind-repo.sh. GitHub Actions variables. Workload Identity.
example: opptra/finance-ops uses finance-ops-deployer in opptra-staging and finance-ops-deployer in its prod project.

the_standard: Work starts from a Linear issue that names the users, the behavior, the production project, and the auth mode: app-login, iap, or public.
why: The agent and the reviewer need a scope. Auth and the prod project decided later turn into a second migration.
how: Open the issue before a branch. Put the link in the pull request. An Openspec file is allowed in the repo and is not required.
tech_stack: Linear. Optional Openspec file.
example: GCC inventory for sales ops. Prod project opptra-datawarehouse. Auth app-login.

the_standard: A new internal tool is one Cloud Run service. FastAPI serves /api and the built UI. Other shapes are named exceptions: a Cloud Run Job, a VM worker, Apps Script, or a config repo with no deploy.
why: One shape is what the workflow, the module, and the agent rules know how to check. A VM for the UI, or Vercel beside GCP, is a second pipeline.
how: Set archetype in service.yaml. The deploy workflow accepts cloud-run-service. A job, a worker, Apps Script, or a config repo follows the written rule until it has its own module.
tech_stack: service.yaml. Archetypes: cloud-run-service, cloud-run-job, vm-worker, apps-script, config-only.
example: A dashboard is cloud-run-service. A scraper worker is vm-worker and its UI stays on Cloud Run.

step: Copy the template and fill service.yaml
the_standard: A new app starts from the template: Python 3.12, uv, Ruff, pytest, FastAPI, Vite, React, TypeScript, one Docker image, and the shared Terraform module. Region is asia-south1.
why: The pipeline can call the same workflows only when the repo has the same manifest, the same infra entrypoint, and the same commands.
how: Copy template/ into a new opptra repo. Fill name, archetype, prod_project, region, and auth. Point infra/main.tf at git::https://github.com/opptra/sdlc.git//modules/cloud-run-service?ref=v1. Run check_manifest.py.
tech_stack: FastAPI. Vite. React. TypeScript. Terraform module modules/cloud-run-service.
example: name gcc-dashboard, prod_project opptra-datawarehouse, region asia-south1, auth app-login.

the_standard: staging and main accept merges only. Each merge needs one human approval and green ci and plan checks. Admins are included. Force-push and branch deletion are off.
why: The deploy workflows run on push to those branches. An unprotected branch means a direct push is a production deploy.
how: Push main, create staging from main, open one pull request so the checks appear, then run scripts/protect-branches.sh. Required checks are ci / ci and plan / plan.
tech_stack: GitHub branch protection. scripts/protect-branches.sh.
example: A direct push to opptra/finance-ops main is rejected.

the_standard: Feature branches come off staging and merge back into staging. main receives code only from a pull request whose source is staging.
why: Production then contains only commits that have already been deployed and looked at in staging.
how: git checkout -b <change> staging. Run the API with uv and the UI with the Vite dev server, which proxies /api to port 8000. Open the pull request with base staging.
tech_stack: git. uvicorn. Vite.
example: Branch add-inventory-filter off staging. The pull request targets staging.

step: Keep the agent on the stack
the_standard: Every app vendors AGENTS.md and .cursor/rules from opptra/sdlc. New UI code is Vite and React. New API code is FastAPI, with routes under /api. The agent does not add a deploy script or a second framework.
why: The model will otherwise copy whatever deploy style is already in the repo. The rules are the constraint that survives a new chat.
how: Copy rules/ into the app when the repo is created. Cursor loads .cursor/rules on each session. opptra-sdlc.mdc is always applied. python.mdc and react.mdc apply by path.
tech_stack: Cursor rules. AGENTS.md. Source directory opptra/sdlc/rules.
example: Asked for a new page, the agent adds a Vite route and a FastAPI route. It does not add Next.js or deploy.sh.

step: Keep secrets out of the repo
the_standard: Secrets live in Secret Manager in the project that runs the service. The image and the git history do not contain them. Staging does not reference a secret whose id ends in _PROD.
why: A secret in git or in an image cannot be unshared. The inventory already has tokens in scripts, HTML, and client images.
how: Create the secret in the target project. Pass the secret id into the service through Terraform when that field exists. Until then, do not commit a .env and do not COPY a credential in the Dockerfile.
tech_stack: Secret Manager.
example: The Uniware token for finance-ops is a prod secret. The staging service has its own secret.

the_standard: Every pull request links a Linear issue and says whether it touches deploy config. Product code and changes to workflows, infra, or service.yaml are separate pull requests.
why: A mixed pull request hides a deploy change inside a feature, and the reviewer looks at the feature.
how: GitHub inserts template/.github/pull_request_template.md. Fill the Linear link and the risk box. Open a second pull request for infra or workflow edits.
tech_stack: GitHub pull request template.
example: The filter PR links the issue and does not edit infra/main.tf. The memory change is its own PR.

the_standard: A merge requires Ruff, the frontend typecheck, and ESLint. Pytest is required once the repo has tests. New apps have a test from the first commit.
why: Lint is the check that is the same in every repo. Leaving it optional is why several apps still have no CI.
how: The app workflow calls opptra/sdlc/.github/workflows/ci.yml. The job installs uv and Node on a GitHub-hosted runner and runs the commands. Branch protection requires the check named ci / ci.
tech_stack: GitHub Actions. Ruff. ESLint. TypeScript. pytest.
example: The template health test calls /api/health and expects status ok.

the_standard: Every pull request comments a Terraform plan for the project it targets. The comment lists resources to add, change, and destroy. The pull request does not change GCP.
why: gcloud run deploy updates a service and leaves anything else behind. The plan is the list colleagues can read before an apply.
how: plan.yml calls terraform-plan.yml. The runner reads service.yaml, writes tfvars for that commit's image tag, runs terraform plan against gs://<project>-tfstate/<app>, and comments the output. A pull request into staging plans opptra-staging. A pull request into main plans prod_project.
tech_stack: Terraform 1.10.5. Google provider. Module modules/cloud-run-service.
example: The comment shows one change, the image tag. A removed resource shows as a destroy.

the_standard: Dobby posts a brief on every pull request before a person is asked. One human approval is required to merge. Dobby's review does not satisfy that approval.
why: The human's time goes to whether the change is right and what it can break. Style and obvious mistakes are already in the brief and in CI.
how: Dobby follows dobby/review-brief.md: a few lines on the change, a risk line, CI status, at most three files, blocking items, and nits. Blocking items request changes. Nits do not. Branch protection requires one approval and dismisses it when new commits are pushed.
tech_stack: Dobby. GitHub branch protection. Spec dobby/review-brief.md.
example: The brief says infra changed, CI is green, nothing blocking. One maintainer approves.

the_standard: A change to workflows, service.yaml, infra, auth, billing, finance, or migrations needs the named owner in addition to the one human approval.
why: Those paths are where a bad merge changes production access, a secret, or what Terraform will destroy.
how: CODEOWNERS lists the paths and the owners. Replace @opptra/platform with real usernames or a real team, then enable code-owner review on the protected branches.
tech_stack: GitHub CODEOWNERS.
example: A React-only pull request needs one approval. A pull request that edits infra/main.tf also needs the platform owner.

step: Build the image and apply on merge to staging
the_standard: Merging to staging builds the image, pushes it to Artifact Registry in the staging project, and applies Terraform. Apply makes the project match infra/. The service answers /api/health.
why: The image has to exist before Cloud Run can run it, and the apply is the step that records what was created so the next plan can show a real diff.
how: Push to staging triggers deploy.yml, which calls deploy-cloud-run.yml on a GitHub-hosted runner. The runner builds the Dockerfile, pushes the SHA tag to asia-south1-docker.pkg.dev/opptra-staging/apps/<name>, runs terraform plan, applies that plan, curls /api/health, and comments the URL.
tech_stack: GitHub Actions. Docker. Artifact Registry. Terraform. Cloud Run, 1 CPU, 512Mi, port 8080.
example: Merge commit abc123 becomes the image gcc-dashboard:abc123 and the Cloud Run revision in opptra-staging.

the_standard: A person opens the staging URL and reads the production plan before opening the pull request from staging to main.
why: CI proves the tests and the plan. It does not prove the feature is the one the Linear issue asked for.
how: The staging job comments the URL. The promotion pull request template has a checkbox for that URL and for the prod plan. The reviewer looks at both.
tech_stack: Cloud Run URL. GitHub pull request template.
example: Open the staging service, try the new filter, then read the prod plan comment before merging to main.

the_standard: Production is a merge from staging to main. That merge builds the same way and applies in prod_project. The pull request is the only approval. The image tag is the commit SHA.
why: A second button, or a laptop script, becomes the path people use when the pipeline is slow. The SHA tag is what the plan and a later revert refer to.
how: The promotion pull request plans prod_project. On merge, deploy-cloud-run.yml builds, pushes to that project's apps repository, and applies gs://<prod-project>-tfstate/<app>. The health check runs again.
tech_stack: The same deploy workflow. service.yaml field prod_project.
example: Merge to main applies gcc-dashboard in opptra-datawarehouse with the merge commit as the image tag.

the_standard: A rollback is a revert that travels through staging and then main. The pipeline applies the reverted commit. There is no direct redeploy of an older tag to production.
why: The reverted commit is reviewed and planned like any other change, so production still matches git and the state file.
how: Branch off staging, git revert the bad commit, merge to staging, check the URL, then merge staging to main. The plan shows the image tag moving back.
tech_stack: git revert. The normal plan and apply workflows.
example: Revert abc123. Staging applies the parent commit. Main applies it next.

when_it_happens: After the app is in production
the_standard: Every new app logs JSON to stdout with severity, message, service, and environment. Cloud Run stores that stream. There is no sidecar.
why: One log shape is what an alert and a person can query across apps. A second library in each repo drifts.
how: The template calls configure_logging() at startup. The deploy sets APP_ENV and SERVICE_NAME. Cloud Logging reads stdout.
tech_stack: Python logging. Cloud Logging.
example: An exception is a line with severity ERROR and service gcc-dashboard.

when_it_happens: After the app is in production
the_standard: Each service has three alerts to the Slack channel for its GCP project: 5xx above 1 percent for five minutes, no ready revision, and application ERROR logs.
why: A deploy can be green and the service can still be down or erroring. These three say which of those happened.
how: After the first successful apply, create the policies in docs/alerting.md in that project and attach the project's Slack channel. One channel per project.
tech_stack: Cloud Monitoring. Slack.
example: The staging channel receives opptra-staging alerts. The warehouse channel receives opptra-datawarehouse alerts.

when_it_happens: After the app is in production
the_standard: New apps ship with a no-op track() function. Product analytics is added in that function after a tool is chosen. No other SDK is added before that.
why: Usage is a real gap, and dropping a vendor into every new app before the choice is made creates another thing to remove.
how: Call track() from the UI when an event matters. The implementation stays empty until the PostHog trial, then the client is written only in frontend/src/analytics.ts.
tech_stack: frontend/src/analytics.ts. PostHog is the candidate.
example: A button calls track('filter_applied'). Today that function returns immediately.

when_it_happens: After the app is in production
the_standard: A production bug is a Linear issue on that app. The fix uses the same feature branch, staging, and main path. There is no production hotfix from a laptop.
why: A hotfix that skips staging is how the laptop deploy path comes back.
how: Open the issue, branch off staging, and promote through the normal pull requests.
tech_stack: Linear.
example: The prod filter is wrong. The issue links the bad revision SHA. The fix merges to staging, then to main.

when_it_happens: When an old app is brought over
step: Add the contract before changing how it runs
the_standard: An existing app keeps its language and gains service.yaml, infra, the workflows, and the agent rules. The old deploy script stays until staging has been applied once through GitHub, then it is removed.
why: Changing the host, the database, and the pipeline in one pull request makes the first plan impossible to read.
how: Follow docs/migrating.md in order: add the files, turn on lint, bind the repo, apply staging, apply production, delete the laptop script. Leave a VM, Vercel, or a database move for a later change.
tech_stack: The same workflows. The app's current language.
example: finance-ops stays FastAPI. After the GitHub apply works, scripts/deploy-staging.sh is deleted.

when_it_happens: When an old app is brought over
the_standard: A service that already exists is imported into Terraform state before the first apply. The first plan is an update.
why: Without the import, Terraform plans a second Cloud Run service next to the live one.
how: From infra/, init the state bucket and prefix, then terraform import the Cloud Run service and the runtime service account using the addresses in docs/resources.md. Open the pull request and confirm the plan says update.
tech_stack: terraform import.
example: Import finance-ops in asia-south1 before the first staging apply.

when_it_happens: When an app needs a database or a worker
step: Database and the shapes that are not the default
the_standard: Postgres is Cloud SQL with prevent_destroy. A VM runs only a worker that cannot be a request. A batch image update does not start a backfill. Apps Script prod clasp runs from main after a staging clasp. Config repos do not deploy.
why: These shapes are real in the inventory. Treating them as the default would make every app carry a pipeline it does not need.
how: Add Cloud SQL in that app's infra with lifecycle prevent_destroy when the app needs a database. Leave Jobs, the VM worker, and Apps Script on the written rule until a module exists. Do the runtime move only after the app already deploys through the standard workflow.
tech_stack: Cloud SQL Postgres 16. Cloud Run Jobs, a VM, and Apps Script are later.
example: SCM's Postgres leaves the VM for Cloud SQL after the app is already deploying through GitHub.
